cards.title: Build the Business Case for Speed with Conversion and Bounce Benchmarks
cards.summary: Use load-time thresholds and revenue math to justify speed work on PDPs, category pages and checkout to stakeholders.
cards.use_when: You need to prioritize a speed initiative against other roadmap items and must translate load time into revenue impact for merchandising, PDP or category page work.
steps: Anchor the case on source-cited conversion effects: a 1-second reduction in load time correlates with roughly a 5.6% conversion increase and nearly a 12% bounce-rate decrease. Mobile-specific figures are slightly different (1-second improvement associated with ~5.9% conversion lift and ~9% bounce reduction), so use the mobile set when the business is mobile-heavy.

Frame the failure thresholds shoppers abandon at: 40% leave after 3 seconds, 63% bounce past 4 seconds, and roughly two-thirds leave at 6 seconds. For page views, 2-second pages average 8.9 pages per session versus 3.3 pages at 8 seconds.

Illustrate with concrete own-store arithmetic rather than generic percentages: daily sessions x conversion rate x AOV gives current daily revenue; recompute with the improved conversion rate to size the annualized gain.

Note that the source's $1.8M/$5.5M example assumes 50,000 daily visitors, 3.5% conversion and $50 AOV with a 6-second average load; treat it as a worked example, not a forecast, and re-run with your own traffic and margin.
Pair revenue upside with ranking and loyalty effects (fast sites appear higher in results; 65% trust a business less after a problem) so the case isn't purely conversion-based.
caveats: Conversion lift figures are observed correlations across studies, not guaranteed causal outcomes for every store; your mileage will vary by traffic quality, device mix and catalog.
Do not present the source's hypothetical revenue scenario as your store's expected result.

cards.title: Adopt Google Core Web Vitals Thresholds as Speed Targets
cards.summary: Set TTFB, FID and FCP targets from source-cited Google benchmarks and check current averages before optimizing.
cards.use_when: You are setting performance budgets or audit criteria for PDP, category and landing page templates and need concrete numbers.
steps: Use Google's recommended thresholds as the pass line: TTFB under 800ms, FID under 100ms, and FCP under 1.8 seconds.
Compare against reported averages to see how much room exists: average TTFB is about 1.286s desktop and 2.594s mobile; average FID is ~12.73ms desktop and ~59.73ms mobile.

Recognize that 'fully loaded' is a different, much larger figure than FCP: average full load is 10.3 seconds desktop and 27.3 seconds mobile, so don't confuse interactive/usable states with paint times.
Check scores with Google's PageSpeed Insights (verify current interface), as the source did, which brought one homepage's FCP to 0.8 seconds.
Route fixes to the right owner: perceived-speed and benchmark work here, technical implementation (minification, image compression, lazy loading) to the technical execution workstream.
caveats: FID has been superseded in Google's current Core Web Vitals program (INP now captures interaction responsiveness); verify the current metric set before committing targets.
These are Google recommendation thresholds, not store-specific targets; derive your own from template and device-mix data.

cards.title: Prioritize the Product and Category Templates Most Shopper Time Spends On
cards.summary: PDPs and category pages carry 72% of page views, so optimize those templates first and quantify time saved per journey.
cards.use_when: You must decide which templates to make faster first with limited engineering capacity.
steps: Focus first on PDP and category templates because they account for 72% of page views in the shopper journey, maximizing the speed benefit per fix.
Set a concrete target using the source comparison: unoptimized PDPs average 6.1 seconds, optimized ones average 4.1 seconds — a full 2 seconds faster.
Quantify the journey-level time saved: with retail's high 5.01 pages per session on desktop, optimized sites save about 23 seconds per shopper journey. That compounds across the funnel.
Treat mobile PDPs as the highest-value target since mobile is ~59% of traffic and pages load 87.8% longer on mobile than desktop on average.
Track pages per session and bounce as secondary KPIs alongside conversion so you capture engagement, not just orders.
caveats: Figures are industry averages reported in the source; benchmark your own templates before assuming the same gap.
Time-saved estimates depend on your pages-per-session figure, which varies by catalog and traffic source.

cards.title: Diagnose and Prepare for IT Brownouts During High-Traffic Sales
cards.summary: High traffic causes dynamic-area slowdowns (cart, login, search), not just crashes; mitigate with queueing and load planning.
cards.use_when: You are planning a flash sale, Black Friday event or product drop and need to protect cart, checkout and login reliability.
steps: Understand brownouts: traffic-induced slowdowns or errors in dynamic areas like add-to-cart, site search and login — not a full outage. They show up as laggy or broken funnel steps during spikes.
Use the Pet Smart Black Friday case as a pattern to plan against: load speed nearly doubled from 7.7s to 13.84s under peak traffic. Test your own peak-load behavior before the event, not during it.
Expect brownouts to be common: 50% of ecommerce consumers report slowdowns during high-traffic occasions, and 82% of those couldn't access the target site at all.

Deploy virtual waiting rooms for limited-inventory events: the source cites 87% of consumers preferring a short queue over a slow/buggy site, 84% preferring a queue to a crash page, and willingness to wait an average of 53 minutes for limited-inventory sales.
Map high-risk funnel steps (cart, checkout, login, search) and define degradation behavior — queue, throttle or static fallback — before traffic hits.

Account for business cost: organizations with frequent outages/brownouts face up to 16x higher costs, and 31% of IT professionals report brand damage and 30% report stock-price impact from these events.
caveats: Queueing trades immediate access for reliability; it is best suited to genuinely high-demand events or limited inventory, not everyday traffic.
The willingness-to-wait and preference percentages are survey opinions from the source, useful for planning rationale but not guarantees of shopper behavior.
Server architecture and load-balancer work belongs with the infrastructure owner, not this playbook.

cards.title: Set Mobile-Specific Speed Standards Separate from Desktop
cards.summary: Mobile pages load far slower and have higher bounce, so judge speed on mobile metrics and set mobile-specific thresholds.
cards.use_when: You are auditing storefront performance or setting pass/fail thresholds for a mobile-first audience.
steps: Treat mobile as the primary performance surface: ~59% of web traffic is mobile, and pages take 87.8% longer to load on mobile on average.
Set abandonment-aware thresholds: 53% of mobile visitors leave past 3 seconds, 64% expect under 4 seconds, and 74% abandon past 5 seconds.
Compare mobile against desktop honestly: mobile bounce averages 56.8% versus 50% on desktop, and mobile users' top complaint (46%) is waiting for pages to load.

Account for the perception gap: 85% of mobile users expect pages to load as fast or faster than desktop, which almost never happens, so perceived mobile speed is a loyalty lever (95% of mobile users return to a fast site vs. 62% for a slow one).
Use mobile-specific conversion figures (1-second mobile improvement ~5.9% conversion lift) when valuing mobile work.
Watch the source's caveat that mobile sites average much worse load times, so desktop-only testing understates the real shopper experience.
caveats: Average mobile load times cited (up to ~15 seconds for some measures, 27.3s full load) are industry averages and will differ substantially by storefront.
Do not apply desktop benchmarks to mobile passes; use separate mobile targets.

cards.title: Reduce Page Weight and Third-Party Script Load to Cut Load Time
cards.summary: Compression and script discipline are constrained by known page-weight and script-cost figures you can plan against.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to prune scripts or compress media as part of a speed budget for PDPs and landing pages.
steps: Count third-party scripts and treat each as a cost: every third-party script adds an average of 34.1 milliseconds to load time, so removing or deferring a handful compounds.
Target compression of images and text: 25% of pages could save more than 250kb, and 10% could save more than 1mb from this alone.
Note that large pages take 318% longer to visually load than small pages, making page weight a first-order lever for visual speed.
Recognize the trade-off shoppers accept: half of users would give up animation and video for faster loads, so heavy hero media is a candidate for trimming.
Connect speed to revenue: the source cites Yahoo gaining 9% traffic from a 0.4-second speedup and the BBC losing ~10% of users per extra second, as directional evidence that even small gains matter.
caveats: Method details for the page-weight and third-party-script figures are not given in the source; use them as planning approximations.
The Yahoo and BBC results are single-company anecdotes, not generalizable benchmarks.

cards.title: Convert Speed Work from Low Priority into an Urgent Initiative
cards.summary: Marketers recognize speed matters but rarely prioritize it; use the priority gap to frame and defend the case.
cards.use_when: You are trying to get engineering time approved for speed work against feature and animation projects on the roadmap.
steps: Lead with the awareness gap: 81% of marketers know speed impacts conversions but do not prioritize optimization, and only 3% name faster speed as a top priority, while 73% call it somewhat or very urgent.
Frame speed as a conversion, loyalty and ranking lever, not a vanity engineering metric; slow sites waste marketing spend by sending paid and organic traffic to pages that bounce.
Counter the common anti-pattern that changes to ecommerce sites usually add animations and features that make pages slower, not faster, so new features should carry a performance review.
Pick a small set of fixes with clear ownership — for example 57% of marketers cited image/media optimization, 43% backend fixes like caching, and 14% CDN usage — and set measurable load-time targets.
Re-measure after changes using a tool like PageSpeed Insights (verify current interface) and tie results back to conversion and bounce.
caveats: The 81%/3%/73% figures are survey opinions from the source, not operational benchmarks.
Prioritization is an organizational decision; these numbers support the argument but don't guarantee budget.

cards.title: Model Load-Time Revenue Impact Before and After Speed Fixes
cards.summary: Estimate revenue upside by applying the source's conversion lift to your own sessions, conversion rate and AOV.
cards.use_when: You need a defensible number to decide whether speed work is worth the engineering investment for your funnel.
steps: Gather your baselines: daily sessions, current conversion rate, average order value, and average load time.

Compute current daily revenue = sessions x conversion rate x AOV, matching the source's method (its example used 50,000 visitors at 3.5% conversion and $50 AOV, yielding 1,750 orders and $87,500/day).
Apply the source's directional lift: a 1-second improvement is associated with conversion moving from 3.5% to 3.7%, roughly 100 added orders per day on those volumes in the example.
Annualize carefully and label assumptions — the source's $1.8M/year and $5.5M/year figures are illustrative, hypothetical math at 50,000 daily visitors and should not be presented as a forecast.
Add secondary value the example excludes: better Google rankings, loyalty, and word-of-mouth, plus the fact that conversion rates are highest (~3.05%) on 1-2 second pages.
caveats: The source itself flags the $1.8M-$5.5M scenario as arbitrary hypothetical math tied to 50,000 daily visitors; use your own inputs.
Conversion lift is an observed correlation across studies, not a guaranteed causal effect of your specific change.

cards.title: Use Load-Time Tiers to Predict Bounce and Browsing Depth
cards.summary: Load-time bands correlate with predictable bounce-rate and pages-per-session shifts, useful for setting speed SLAs.
cards.use_when: You are setting load-time SLAs or diagnosing why bounce and session depth move, and need reference bands.
steps: Use the cited bands as planning heuristics: going from 1 to 3 seconds raises bounce chance by ~32%, 1 to 5 seconds by ~90%, and 1 to 10 seconds by ~123%.
Pair with absolute averages: pages under 2 seconds average ~9% bounce, while pages at 5 seconds average ~38%.
Expect browsing depth to fall with load time: 8.9 pages per session at 2 seconds versus 3.3 pages at 8 seconds.
Connect the bands back to revenue levers: deeper sessions mean more PDP and category views, which the source shows account for 72% of shopper-journey page views.
Set an internal SLA inside Google's 3-second mobile recommendation with headroom, since shoppers increasingly expect faster and fast pages are where the highest conversion rates cluster.
caveats: The band figures are aggregate averages across many sites, not targets for any specific storefront.
Bounce and pages-per-session are also affected by traffic source, price and catalog depth, so speed is one factor, not the sole driver.

cards.title: Translate a Slow Site's Behavioral Damage into Retention and Word-of-Mouth Risk
cards.summary: Quantify how slow pages deter purchases, repeat visits and referrals, not just immediate bounces.
cards.use_when: You are making the retention and brand case for speed to leadership, beyond single-session conversion.
steps: Use the source's post-slowdown behavior shares: 45.4% of shoppers are less likely to make a purchase, 36.8% are less likely to return, and 11.9% are likely to tell a friend — framing speed as a retention and acquisition issue.
Incorporate abandonment behavior during a slow load: about 50% refresh once, 22% close the tab, and 14% visit a competitor.
Reinforce trust stakes: 65% of consumers trust a business less after a problem, 64% shop elsewhere after a poor experience, and 1 in 3 leave a brand they love after one bad experience.
Set a first-page-speed target as a ranking and discoverability lever, since first-page Google results average 1.96 seconds to load (directionally: faster may rank better).
Connect to loyalty value: 95% of mobile users return to a fast site versus 62% for a slow site, making speed a repeat-purchase input.
caveats: These are survey percentages around hypothetical or recalled experiences, not store-observed churn rates.
The ranking claim is inferential in the source (slow sites rank lower) and not a confirmed algorithm rule.
